Reproduce failing CI mode with pinned inputs; compare plugin versions.

prompt: After a plugin update, claude -p fails in CI while an interactive local session succeeds on the same repository and prompt. The last known-good plugin version is available. What investigation should precede a model or prompt change?

constraints: The failure occurs before an HTTP response.
DNS, proxy, and TLS evidence is available.
No provider request identifier or response body exists.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If an HTTP response and request ID were present, preserve that ID and classify the documented response before choosing retry or owner routing.
details.errorCorrection: A provider status check or escalation can be recorded later, but bounded HTTP retry and alternate-runner comparison do not replace diagnosis of the captured pre-response transport failure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic includes a unique request ID in responses and errors so operators can correlate a failing request with their own traces and support investigations. The pre-response transport diagnosis follows the scenario evidence.
details.scenarioApplication: Preserve DNS/proxy/TLS evidence, verify the failing runner and destination configuration, reproduce there, and defer provider request-ID analysis until an HTTP response exists.
details.transfer: Choose the diagnostic layer supported by the evidence: transport before response, provider correlation after a response and request identifier.

messages.text: Status or escalation with a timestamp may support a later incident, but the captured DNS, proxy, and TLS failure must be diagnosed before assigning it to provider execution.
HTTP retry-after semantics apply to a response; with no response received, retrying before transport diagnosis does not establish provider execution or repair the runner path.
A second runner can be useful after preserving the evidence, but comparing provider behavior first changes the experiment before the failing runner's transport path is understood.

feedback.reason: No response was received to correlate, so the evidence is at the runner transport boundary; provider request-ID analysis becomes relevant only after an HTTP response is received.

course.title: Enterprise Integration & Production: Architect Module 2
course.section: M2-S11: Enterprise integration patterns: identity, auth, data, and observability

options.text: Assign the failure to provider execution from the timestamp alone.
Diagnose the runner’s DNS, proxy, and TLS before provider attribution.
Apply HTTP retry-after semantics despite receiving no HTTP response.
Compare provider behavior elsewhere before inspecting the failing transport.

prompt: A CI job fails before receiving any HTTP response. DNS resolution and TLS/proxy diagnostics are captured, while no provider request identifier or response error body exists. What diagnostic layer comes first?

constraints: Safe mode removes customizations but leaves core execution and managed controls active.
The clean user/project comparison succeeds.
Managed policy and environment state must remain in force.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If both safe mode and clean user/project configuration failed after managed policy and environment checks matched, repository, runtime, or external-service investigation would be justified.
details.errorCorrection: Managed-policy, plugin, or authentication checks can support later escalation, but fixed core controls and clean user/project success first localize the repair to the user/project layer.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic notes that safe mode disables customizations while authentication, model, built-in tools, permissions, and managed hooks/settings remain; comparing a clean configuration isolates user and project settings. Keeping managed controls is scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Compare and correct the implicated user or project setting, preserve managed policy, rerun the bounded task, and escalate externally only if the clean configuration and managed/environment checks also fail.
details.transfer: Use a clean user/project comparison to isolate configuration layers, and keep managed controls fixed while deciding whether external escalation is warranted.

messages.text: The controlled comparison succeeds under the same managed policy, so changing that policy targets a layer not implicated by this evidence.
The clean user/project success already distinguishes the implicated configuration layer; further plugin bisection treats fixed safe-mode evidence as unresolved external evidence.
Authentication and provider access were unchanged during the contrast; another-runner check can follow only if the clean configuration and managed/environment checks also fail.

feedback.reason: Safe mode alone does not prove an external cause: the clean user/project success isolates those configuration layers while authentication, built-ins, permissions, and managed controls remain unchanged.

course.title: Team Enablement and Operational Productivity: Architect Module 5
course.section: M5-S06: Supporting debugging and operational issue resolution

options.text: Change managed policy despite clean user/project success with policy unchanged.
Bisect plugins even though clean user/project configuration already succeeds.
Repair the isolated user/project layer and verify with policy fixed.
Change authentication on another runner before correcting isolated settings.

prompt: A failure remains in safe mode, but a clean user and project configuration makes the same bounded task succeed. Authentication, model, built-in tools, permissions, managed hooks, and managed settings remain unchanged during the comparison. What should be repaired?

constraints: Lower-sensitivity metadata and redacted reproduction were tried first.
Authorization, access, restricted storage, and deletion controls are recorded.
Routine telemetry does not need prompt retention.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Without named authorization, restricted storage, or a deletion rule, remain with redacted metadata and safe-mode reproduction rather than collecting detailed diagnostics.
details.errorCorrection: Normal full capture creates unnecessary exposure, while blanket refusal ignores a proportionate authorized investigation; indefinite retention exceeds the approved purpose and deletion boundary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends safe mode first and explains that detailed diagnostics or heap snapshots can contain conversation content and credentials, so sensitive captures require careful handling. Authorization, purpose, and retention are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Capture only the approved sample in restricted storage with named access, use it for the bounded reproduction, delete it on the agreed schedule, and keep routine logs redacted.
details.transfer: Escalate sensitive diagnostics only through an authorized, purpose-limited capture with controlled access and deletion, while routine telemetry remains redacted.

messages.text: Routine incident logs would expose sensitive prompts and heap material beyond the authorized bounded purpose.
The authorization is purpose-limited to the stated reproduction; it does not grant unrestricted reuse in other investigations.
Indefinite unrestricted collection violates purpose limitation and the recorded access and deletion boundary.
Without restricted storage, named access, and a deletion boundary, the capture is not a controlled exception to the redacted default.
Without bounded use, deletion, and redacted routine telemetry, the sensitive sample can persist or spread beyond the incident.

feedback.reason: Detailed diagnostics are justified only as a bounded, explicitly authorized exception after redacted evidence is insufficient; storage, access, purpose, deletion, and redacted defaults keep the exposure controlled.

course.title: Team Enablement and Operational Productivity: Architect Module 5
course.section: M5-S06: Supporting debugging and operational issue resolution

options.text: Limit capture to the authorized sample, storage, named access, and deletion date.
Use it only for the reproduction; delete as agreed and keep routine logs redacted.
Add full prompt and heap captures to routine incident logs for future support.
Reuse the sample for unrelated incidents without checking purpose authorization.
Keep an unrestricted capture indefinitely to reuse across later incidents.

prompt: Metadata and redacted timing are insufficient to reproduce a high-memory incident. The organization has explicitly authorized a private diagnostic sample with a named operator, restricted storage, and deletion date; support does not need routine prompt retention. Select TWO actions.

constraints: The provider response and transport status are valid.
The consumer schema version and parser error are available.
The failure occurs at the downstream contract boundary.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If the provider response were invalid or an HTTP error reached CI before parsing, provider error classification and request correlation would be the relevant diagnostic branch.
details.errorCorrection: Provider retries, model changes, and timeouts cannot repair a consumer that rejects a valid response; accepting both schemas without versioning moves the failure downstream.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends claude -p for CI and scripts, structured output for programmatic processing, and restricted tools when running unattended. Versioning the consumer contract and adding a test are scenario controls.
details.scenarioApplication: Compare both schema versions, update the consumer or restore a compatible producer through the authorized change process, then test the agreed contract and rerun CI.
details.transfer: When transport and provider output are valid but a consumer rejects the schema, repair and test the versioned interface at the producer-consumer boundary.

messages.text: Availability is normal and the response is valid, so provider retries or model changes do not repair the older consumer contract.
A permissive unversioned parser hides incompatible fields and leaves downstream behavior undefined instead of establishing an accepted schema.
Timeouts and repeated valid responses cannot resolve a schema-version mismatch in the CI consumer.

feedback.reason: The response meets its requested schema, but the consumer expects another version. Align the versioned interface and test the actual CI boundary instead of retrying valid responses.

course.title: Team Enablement and Operational Productivity: Architect Module 5
course.section: M5-S06: Supporting debugging and operational issue resolution

options.text: Retry or switch models while preserving the incompatible consumer schema.
Align the versioned producer-consumer schema and rerun contract tests.
Accept either schema unversioned and leave downstream jobs to find conflicts.
Increase timeouts instead of examining the explicit consumer schema error.

prompt: The provider returns a response that passes the requested structured-output schema, but the CI consumer rejects it because the consumer still expects an older field version. Request latency and provider availability are normal. What should be repaired first?

constraints: The native-versus-JavaScript memory classification is available.
The JavaScript heap is within its normal range.
Lower-sensitivity runtime and repository evidence can be collected first.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If JavaScript heap usage dominated and remained high after safe-mode and clean-session checks, a private heap snapshot could be appropriate under the documented sensitive-data handling.
details.errorCorrection: A detailed JavaScript artifact does not explain native allocations, while model changes or routine heap capture change or broaden the investigation without addressing the measured resource class.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic's troubleshooting guidance says to try safe mode first, distinguish JavaScript-heap from native-memory pressure, and handle any heap snapshot as sensitive diagnostic data. The native investigation order is scenario policy.
details.scenarioApplication: Preserve the classification, inspect the native-memory path and bounded repository/runtime reproduction, and reserve a restricted JavaScript heap snapshot for a case with measured JavaScript heap growth.
details.transfer: Choose diagnostics by measured resource class; reserve sensitive, detailed artifacts for the class they can actually explain.

messages.text: A JavaScript heap snapshot targets the normal heap, not the measured native allocations, and it creates sensitive data without a matched diagnostic question.
Changing the model or heap allocation does not identify whether native or JavaScript memory causes the incident and can obscure the bounded reproduction.
Discarding the available memory classification and collecting routine heap data broadens sensitive capture while ignoring the native evidence.

feedback.reason: The measured memory class makes an ordinary JavaScript heap snapshot low-yield; native-memory evidence directs the next investigation to runtime or repository loading while sensitive capture remains conditional.

course.title: Team Enablement and Operational Productivity: Architect Module 5
course.section: M5-S06: Supporting debugging and operational issue resolution

options.text: Take a full JS snapshot first despite the measured native-memory growth.
Investigate native memory; reserve JS snapshots for JS-heap questions.
Change model or heap limits before investigating the measured native pressure.
Discard memory classification and collect full heap snapshots for every incident.

prompt: A bounded reproduction still shows high memory after safe mode and a clean session. Diagnostics indicate native allocations dominate while the JavaScript heap remains within its normal range; the team proposes taking a JavaScript heap snapshot first. What is the best next diagnostic?

constraints: Project-root files, relative command paths, and active configuration sources are inspectable.
The existing setup can be examined without resetting it.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: If both directories loaded identical configuration and logs identified an authentication failure, credential repair would become the appropriate next step.
details.errorCorrection: Moving configuration can conceal a project-root defect, while credential refresh and reinstall change components shared by both sessions without first explaining the directory difference.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic recommends /mcp for connection and approval status, targeted MCP debug logging, and checking project paths and relative commands when servers fail.
details.scenarioApplication: Confirm which project configuration is loaded in each directory, inspect the server’s approval and connection status, check relative commands, and enable narrowly targeted diagnostics if necessary.
details.transfer: Use the smallest observed environment difference to choose the first diagnostic comparison.

messages.text: User scope might mask the symptom while broadening the integration to unrelated projects; it does not establish why the project setup differs.
The shared account works in the other directory, so refresh is a weaker first hypothesis than the configuration and approval differences that can be inspected.
A clean executable can help an installation fault, but the same installed version already works in one directory; inspect that contrast before resetting it.

feedback.reason: The directory-dependent behavior is evidence about project discovery, paths, or local approval state. Inspecting those differences is more informative than changing the scope or resetting a shared installation.

course.title: Team Enablement and Operational Productivity: Architect Module 5
course.section: M5-S06: Supporting debugging and operational issue resolution

options.text: Move the integration to user scope instead of explaining the directory contrast.
Refresh the shared account before comparing the different project settings.
Compare project discovery, paths, and /mcp status before resetting.
Reinstall the working CLI before investigating repository-specific configuration.

prompt: A project MCP server appears in Claude Code from one repository directory but is missing from another. A project hook also fails to run in the second directory. Both sessions use the same account and installed version. What should the developer inspect first?

constraints: Request IDs, error types, and attempt counts can be retained.
Repository owners can correct invalid configuration.
Retries must be bounded and failures remain visible.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A documented transient condition may justify a retry even when the request is unchanged; an invalid-request response requires correction before another equivalent attempt.
details.errorCorrection: Universal retry, runner restart, and reduced concurrency can help transient conditions but do not change invalid request configuration.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Anthropic documents distinct error types, retry-after semantics, exponential backoff for transient failures, and a separate spend-cap condition that keeps failing until access resumes.
details.scenarioApplication: Record the error type and request ID, apply documented backoff to eligible transient failures, and terminate malformed requests visibly with enough context for the owning repository to repair them.
details.transfer: Choose recovery from the failure class and changed preconditions, not merely from a nonzero exit status.

messages.text: A bounded loop is better than an unlimited loop, but replaying a known malformed request still wastes attempts and delays the actionable failure.
A clean process does not repair a configuration value that is sent unchanged in every request.
Lower parallelism addresses congestion, whereas the invalid-request class is caused by request configuration rather than load.

feedback.reason: The payloads already distinguish recoverable service conditions from a deterministic request defect. Recovery should use that evidence instead of making every failure consume the same retry budget.

course.title: Team Enablement and Operational Productivity: Architect Module 5
course.section: M5-S06: Supporting debugging and operational issue resolution

options.text: Classify errors; retry eligible failures and expose invalid requests.
Retry every failure to exhaustion before classifying it for the owner.
Restart the runner and repeat unchanged invalid input as if it were transient.
Reduce concurrency and requeue malformed requests without correcting them.

prompt: An unattended Claude Code CI job retries every nonzero exit identically. Its structured error payloads show both transient overload responses and invalid-request failures caused by repository configuration. Which recovery design should replace the current policy?
